Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-15
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Ava Chen (Redwood CSM), Maya Thompson (Voyager VP Eng), Ravi Kapoor (Voyager SRE Lead), Lena Ortiz (Voyager Security), Jon Park (Voyager Product)

--- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) ---
Samira: quick follow-up after incident, recap of fixes and next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we wanted to run through the postmortem follow-up from the June 8th incident. I know some of you already saw the preliminary notes - we'll go through timeline, what we changed, and then action items. Maya, you wanna kick off with any context from Voyager side?
[00:18] Maya: Yeah thanks Samira. Um, quick note - execs are, are worried about recurrence, obviously, so they want us to understand mitigations and timelines. For context, on June 8th we saw a spike in inference requests around 08:14 UTC, and at about 08:18 two things happened: our internal cache eviction overlapped with Redwood's autoscaler spin-up, and we saw a cascade of long-tail latencies.
[00:42] Ravi: Just to add, from SRE view there was a flood of retries from the client side which amplified the load, and then the KV cache cold-start cost a lot of token compute. We had a backlog, and some pods got OOMs on the lower mem nodes.
[01:05] Diego: Right - our investigation shows that the KV cache eviction and the autoscaler threshold being too aggressive created a window where requests were served from cold paths repeatedly. Also we found an edge case in the autoscaler where rapid scale-up did not prebind the GPU context quickly enough, which increased latency.
[01:29] Jon Park: Sorry interject, when you say KV cache, is that keyed-value cache in the gateway or in the model runtime? I think I heard 'K-V cash' in the doc earlier so I wanted to be sure.
[01:40] Diego: Good call, Jon. It's the runtime KV cache inside the inference kernel - the per-shard KV store for attention caches. When those are evicted we pay the full token decode again until warm.
[01:54] Lena: From security side the question is whether any PII was exposed during retries or logs - we're still reviewing the logs but initial look says no, we had encrypted transport and no payload leaks, but we do want the full audit trail.
[02:12] Samira: Yep we'll share the full request logs and the audit trail, and also the KMS key rotation and HSM notes - I'll attach the security pack.
[02:22] Maya: Thanks. Can you also confirm the impact window and which endpoints? Our PMs saw errors on both /generate and /chat endpoints.
[02:33] Diego: Both endpoints were impacted because they share the same runtime pool for that model variant. The majority of errors were 503s during the scale transition.
[02:43] Ava: Quick note: we've already deployed a temporary circuit breaker at the routing layer to fail fast when queue depth crosses 350ms SLO breach - Diego can speak to the exact config.
[02:57] Diego: Yeah we added a circuit breaker that returns a graceful degraded response and triggers rate-limit throttling upstream; it's been live since 06/10 and we've seen the 99th percentile latency return to normal in our monitoring. There's some noise at 99.9p but overall things look much improved.
[03:16] Ravi: That's promising. Do you have numbers - was cost impacted heavily during the event? Execs asked about unit economics.
[03:25] Samira: We saw an increase in token compute cost for that day - roughly 2.8x for the affected window due to retries and cold-path cost. We're recommending a post-incident cost report which I'll send.
[03:36] Maya: On mitigations front besides the circuit breaker, what else did Redwood change?
[03:41] Diego: We tightened autoscale thresholds, added a warm-up prebind for GPUs when scale event detected (pre-allocate contexts), and adjusted the eviction TTL on the KV cache to be more conservative for this workload. Also added a short-term sticky routing to keep hot traffic on warm hosts.
[04:02] Jon Park: Does sticky routing risk imbalanced load across hosts?
[04:07] Diego: There's a tradeoff - we keep a small percentage sticky (10-15%) so most traffic still balances. It's configurable by route.
[04:15] Maya: We also need an updated runbook. Our oncall had to improvise steps and they'd like a step-by-step.
[04:22] Ava: We're publishing a revised runbook tonight, it will include play-by-play for detection, mitigation commands, and rollback steps. We'll include the alert thresholds and recommended SLOs.
[04:33] Samira: Great. Lena - from security are there any blockers to the runbook or the logs you need?
[04:40] Lena: Just ensure logs include request IDs and the KMS key material references - we need the audit trace to match our compliance process. Also, remind me about SSO/SAML session enforcement during incidents, we had a question on whether tokens persisted across pod restarts.
[04:58] Diego: Tokens are validated by your IdP, but we cache a short-lived session token at the gateway; that survives restart only if session store persisted. We recommended not to rely on that for auth during incidents, revalidate upstream.
[05:12] Maya: Ok, next - runbooks and bench tests. Diego, you mentioned a dedicated capacity bench?
[05:18] Diego: Yes, we propose running a dedicated capacity benchmark with Voyager's traffic pattern using your spike traces. We'll spin up a dedicated small pool to replicate the June 8th pattern and measure tail latency and how autoscaler behaves. Target is to validate sticky routing + prebind reduces 99.9p by >50%.
[05:38] Ravi: We'll share the logs and synthetic traces from the 08:14 window.
[05:45] Samira: Perfect. We'll also run a canary on the runbook automation so your oncall can rehearse.
[05:52] Maya: One more question on security: SOC2 scope - does the change to cache TTLs or sticky routing affect our compliance boundary?
[06:00] Samira: No change to boundary; these are runtime configuration changes. We'll include the config diffs in the SOC2 artifact we share.
[06:08] Jon Park: Any talk of moving to private deployment or VPC to reduce blast radius? Execs asked if Dedicated or Private would have prevented this.
[06:17] Samira: Good question - dedicated capacity can reduce noisy neighbor risk and give you more predictable scaling because you control the pool size; but the specific root cause here (cache eviction + autoscaler edge) would need similar mitigations even on private. However Private + Dedicated together give more knobs: you can pin model variants, reserve warm hosts, and have stricter autoscale controls.
[06:38] Maya: So what's the recommended path? Short term: keep hosted, apply mitigations; medium term: pilot dedicated capacity for critical flows?
[06:45] Diego: Exactly. Short term mitigations we've applied. Medium term run bench on dedicated and present results; if that looks good, we can propose a reserved capacity plan.
[06:56] Ravi: Cost estimate for dedicated?
[06:59] Samira: We'll send an initial committed pricing scenario depending on size - Diego will run the bench to estimate utilization.
[07:06] Lena: Also want an incident SLA guarantee for rollback performance - basically how fast can you change routing or disable a model variant.
[07:15] Diego: We can implement a fast rollback flag at the control plane - typically sub 60s to flip routing to a fallback variant, depending on propagation. We'll document that in the runbook.
[07:28] Ava: Quick note on monitoring - we added a new alert for KV cache miss rate and a synthetic probe for both /generate and /chat endpoints at 1m intervals. That should surface regressions faster.
[07:42] Maya: Nice. Any outstanding unknowns?
[07:45] Ravi: One unknown is the autoscaler edge case under mixed workloads; we need bench results to confirm the prebind behavior under your exact mix of short and long sequences.
[07:58] Diego: Agreed. We'll also test with aggressive retry patterns to measure amplification and show rate-limiter efficacy.
[08:06] Jon Park: On the communications side, we'll need a short exec summary for our leadership and a more detailed tech postmortem for our eng org.
[08:16] Samira: We'll prepare both - the exec summary and full timeline + root cause + mitigations + next steps.
[08:22] Maya: Okay that sounds good. Can we recap next steps quickly?
[08:27] Samira: Sure - Diego to run bench on dedicated (target 06/25); Ava to publish runbook (06/18); Samira to send SOC2/KMS/HSM docs (06/17); Ravi to share traffic traces (06/19). Follow-up call week of 06/29.
[08:44] Jon Park: Thanks all.
[08:46] Maya: Thanks, appreciate the quick response.
[08:49] Lena: Thanks, bye.
[08:50] Samira: Bye everyone.

--- End transcript ---
